dataset.name: Trace Metal Content and Speciation, Water and Soil Chemistry, and Methane Production for a Wetland in Missouri (September 2015) and in Florida (January 2016)
description: Data is associated with a manuscript in preparation for submission to explore whether low trace metal availability inhibits methane production in freshwater wetland soils. Reported data are from two field sites, one in Missouri and the second in Florida (see location data). At each site, surface water compositions and properties and soil compositions are reported. Trace metal availability is assessed via sequential chemical extractions, Ni K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy, and X-ray microfluorescence imaging. Soil mineralogy is determined via powder X-ray diffraction. Multi-energy X-ray microfluorescence imaging as well as bulk and microscale S K-edge XANES spectra assess sulfur speciation in the soils. This package also reports data from trace metal amendment experiments, specifically methane (CH4) production versus time in soil incubations, the dissolved trace metal concentrations in these incubations, and the Ni K-edge XANES and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra of soils to which increasing concentrations of Ni were added. A final version of this package will be published upon acceptance of the associated manuscript.

measurementTechnique:
Field Sampling and Site Information:
Two freshwater wetland sites were investigated at Marais Temps Clair Conservation Area, Saint Charles County, Missouri, USA (Site Missouri) and the Arboretum of the University of Central Florida, Orlando, Florida, USA (Site Florida). The Missouri site (38°54’17”N 90°24’30”W) consists of an elongated 10,000 m2 stream-fed marsh partially enclosed by levees. Three sampling locations (38°54’19.56”N 90°24’29.62”W, 38°54’16.21”N 90°24’29.28”W, 38°54’14.58”N 90°24’29.09”W, all WGS 84) were selected in September 2015 along the flow direction of water through the site. Soils at the site consist of a thin (2-5 cm) peat layer overlying silty clay. The Florida wetland site (28°35’34”N 81°10’41”W) consists of a depressional cypress dome fed by both precipitation and groundwater. The 12,000 m2 elliptical wetland is located in east central Florida within the University of Central Florida Arboretum and is surrounded by pine flatwoods. Soils at the site consist of a leaf litter layer overlying a 20 cm to 1 m thick muck and peat layer. The entire wetland is underlain by fine sand. Sampling locations were selected in January 2016 along a radial transect from the wetland edge to the center (28°35’28.98”N 81°10’46.20”W, 28°35’30.12”N 81°10’46.32”W, 28°35’30.60”N 81°10’46.32”W, all WGS 84), showing a gradation in water depth (5-60 cm).
At each sampling location, surface waters were first collected using grab sampling in new polypropylene bottles. Subsamples were filtered using sterile, 0.22 µm pore size mixed cellulose ester (MCE) syringe filters connected to sterile polypropylene syringes with polyethylene plungers. A portion of this filtered water was acidified to 2% HNO3 in the field using trace metal grade nitric acid for subsequent analysis of dissolved major elements and trace metals in the laboratory. The unfiltered portion was immediately placed on ice for later analysis of nutrients. A second, larger volume of water (1 to 3 L) was collected in one location at each field site, returned to the laboratory, filtered, and archived at 4°C for later use in experiments.
Following collection of surface water samples, triplicate soil cores were collected at each sampling location using a piston corer with 7.6 cm outer diameter, 7.0 cm inner diameter polycarbonate sampling tubes. Each sample tube recovered ~15 cm of soil with overlying surface water. Samples from the Missouri site were sealed in the field, placed on ice, and returned to the laboratory at Washington University. The soil cores were then extruded in 5 cm increments, placed in polyethylene bags, and immediately transferred into an anaerobic chamber (Coy Laboratory Products, 3% H2/97% N2 atmosphere, <1 ppmv O2) to prevent oxidation. Soil cores from the Florida field site were extruded in the field in 5 cm increments, placed in polyethylene bags, placed on ice, and returned to the laboratory at the University of Central Florida. The samples were then impulse sealed in secondary polyethylene bags that contained oxygen scavenger sachets. These were refrigerated until being shipped on ice overnight to Washington University, where they were also then stored in an anaerobic chamber. All oxygen sachets generated substantial heat after the Florida soil core samples were unpacked and the sachets were brought outside of the anaerobic chamber for disposal. This confirmed that the sample bags maintained anaerobic conditions during transport. Each soil core sample was subsampled for archival and analysis. One quarter of each core sample impulse sealed in polyethylene pouches before storage in a -80°C freezer for long-term archival. The remainder of each soil core sample was retained in an anaerobic chamber for characterization and incubation experiments.
Soil and Water Characterization:
Elemental analysis of the filtered, acidified waters were performed using an Agilent Technologies 7500ce inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometer (ICP-MS) for trace metals and a Perkin Elmer Optima 7300 DV inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) for major elements. Dissolved nutrient analyses were performed via colorimetric methods on filtered, unacidified water samples within hours of collection. For the Missouri wetland water samples, NH4+, NO3-, and PO43- concentrations were measured with a Hach DR 2700TM Portable Spectrophotometer. For the Florida wetland water samples, these species were measured using a Seal AQ2 Automated Discrete Analyzer. Alkalinity was not measured but major cation and anion charge balance calculations yields bicarbonate concentrations of ~10 mM for the Missouri site and ~0.05 mM for the Florida site. Total solid-phase Fe, P, and trace metal contents were determined by microwave-assisted digestion (CEM Mars 6) and analysis by ICP-MS and ICP-OES. Total N and S were determined via combustion elemental analysis using an Elementar vario MACRO cube. Total organic and inorganic carbon were determined using a Shimadzu TOC-L Organic Carbon Analyzer equipped with a SSM-5000A Solid Sample Combustion Unit. Mineralogy was measured by micronizing each sample in a McCrone Micronizing Mill with agate grinding elements followed by analysis via powder X-ray diffraction using a Bruker d8 Advance instrument equipped with a Cu Kα X-ray tube operating at 40 kV and 40 mA and a LynxEye XE energy-dispersive silicon strip detector.
Sequential chemical extractions, conducted in triplicate, employed a modified extraction procedure optimized for use with wetland sediments; operationally-defined pool labels are given in quotations for ease of discussion. The “exchangeable” pool was extracted at room temperature (22±1°C) in 1.0 M magnesium chloride at pH 7 in a water to soil ratio of 8, with the mixture mixed end-over-end for 1 hour. The “weakly sorbed” pool was extracted at room temperature in 1.0 M sodium acetate adjusted to pH 5.0 using acetic acid, again at a water to soil ratio of 8 with a 5 hour mixing time. These first two steps were carried out in the anaerobic chamber to prevent oxidation of extracted Fe(II) by air. The “reducible” pool was extracted at 96°C in 0.04 M hydroxylamine hydrochloride in 25% acetic acid at a water to soil ratio of 10 with a 5 hour heating time. Finally, the “oxidizable” pool was extracted in nitric acid and hydrogen peroxide using a multi-step procedure. First, 3 mL of 0.02 M nitric acid and 5 mL of 30% hydrogen peroxide were added per gram of soil and allowed to react for 2 hours. The samples were then placed in an 85°C oven for 24 hours, at which time an additional 3 mL of 30% hydrogen peroxide per gram of soil was added. The sample was then heated at 85°C for an additional 24 hours. After a 1 hour cooling period, 5 mL of 3.2 M ammonium acetate per gram of soil was added to the sample, which was then mixed end-over-end for 30 minutes at room temperature. At the end of each step, the samples were centrifuged for 10 minutes at 4500 rpm with the fluid then decanted, filtered (0.22 µm MCE), and acidified to 2% nitric acid. The extractions utilized analytical grade salts and trace metal grade nitric acid and hydrogen peroxide.
Soil Incubations:
Anoxic incubations were used to evaluate the impact of trace metal additions, primarily nickel, on methane production by the wetland soils. Initial preparation was conducted in an anaerobic chamber to inhibit aerobic methanotrophy. These studies employed soil materials stored in this chamber prior to the experiments and field site water that was filtered, autoclaved, and then deoxygenated by sparging with ultrahigh purity N2 gas. Dissolved O2 concentrations were below the 2.5 µg/L detection limit of a colorimetric indicator test (CHEMets Kit K-7540). Sets of triplicate incubations were prepared using a 1:3 soil:water ratio (0.5 g soil to 1.5 mL water for the Missouri site, 1.5 g soil to 4.5 mL water for the Florida site) by adding homogenized wet soil from the surface layer (0-5 cm) of a soil core to a 60 mL borosilicate serum bottle, followed by addition of site water. For each field site, five different trace metal additions were prepared, yielding fifteen separate incubations per site. The level of trace metal additions used were determined by preliminary measurements to assess trace metal binding to the soil solids, enabling additions that would generate dissolved trace metal concentrations in the range identified as optimal in pure culture studies of methanogens. Incubations for both sites included a control set with no metal addition plus a range of additions of dissolved nickel (prepared from NiCl2·6H2O), which differed between the Missouri and Florida site because of their distinct capacities to bind metals. One set of incubations for the Florida site used a mixture of Ni, Co, Zn, and Fe (prepared from NiCl2·6H2O, CoCl2·6H2O, ZnCl2, FeCl2·4H2O) to explore whether the low dissolved and solid-phase trace metal concentrations at the site might more broadly inhibit methane production. The bottles were then sealed with sterile blue butyl rubber stoppers and fastened with aluminum crimp caps. The sealed incubation bottles were then removed from the anaerobic chamber and had their headspaces flushed with ultrahigh purity N2 gas using a gassing station to remove H2 from the bottles. These incubations were then stored at ambient temperature (22±1°C) in the dark and inverted to minimize gas leakage.
Headspace methane concentrations were determined on a bi-daily basis for the first two weeks, and then less frequently at longer incubation times. A gas-tight syringe removed 2 mL of headspace gas for each sampling, which was then replaced by an equal volume of ultrahigh purity N2 gas to maintain constant total pressure. Methane concentration in each samples was measured by direct injection into a Shimadzu GC-2014 ATF Gas Chromatograph equipped with a 0.50 m Hayesep T (80/100 mesh) column followed by a 2.0 m Molecular Sieve column 5A (60/80 mesh) followed by a Thermal Conductivity Detector (TCD) and a Flame Ionization Detector (FID). Ar was used as the carrier gas at 5.6 mL/min. Temperature conditions were set at 80.0°C, 100°C, and 250 °C for the oven, TCD, and FID, respectively. Standards of 0.026% - 5.2% methane in nitrogen were prepared by controlled mixing of N2 and CH4 gas sources using a gassing station. Methane concentrations were calculated using the linear regression analysis of a 12-point calibration curve run three times. Three of the standards were run daily to check for instrumental drift; no statistically significant deviations from the calibration curve were observed. Total methane generation was corrected for dissolved CH4 via Henry’s law and for the removal of CH4 during each sampling. At the end of each incubation period, the residual fluid was filtered (0.22 µm MCE membrane) and acidified with trace metal grade nitric acid before analysis for dissolved metals via ICP-MS.
Nickel Binding Mechanisms:
Surface soils (0-5 cm) from the two field sites were suspended in filtered, autoclaved water from the corresponding site in a ratio of 3 mL water/g soil. The water was spiked with various concentrations of dissolved NiCl2 and allowed to react for 7 days while continuously mixed on end-over-end rotators. The solids were then collected on MCE filter membranes with 0.22 µm pore size, with the filtrate acidified with 2% trace metal grade nitric acid. Total Ni uptake on the soil solids was determined by difference between the initial Ni concentration and the final dissolved concentration obtained from ICP-MS analysis of the filtrate. The solids on MCE membranes were prepared for analysis of Ni speciation using X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy. These were enclosed between two Kapton films, which were sealed with Kapton tape and then further impulse sealed in polyethylene bags to prevent oxidation and dehydration. The samples were then shipped to a synchrotron light source for analysis. All sample preparation was performed in an anaerobic chamber.
X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy Data Collection and Analysis:
Ni K-edge X-ray absorption fine-structure (XAFS) spectra were obtained at beamline 20-BM-B at the Advanced Photon Source (APS) and beamline 11-2 at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL). 20-BM-B employs a Si (111) fixed-offset, double-crystal monochromator and 11-2 a Si (220) variable-exit, double-crystal monochromator, with the second crystal at both beamlines detuned 10-20% to reduce the harmonic content of the beam. 20-BM-B also utilizes a toroidal Si mirror with an Al2O3 on Pt bilayer coating for focusing to a <1 mm spot size and a flat Rh-coated Si mirror for additional harmonic rejection, both located after the monochromator. 11-2 uses a flat Rh-coated mirror before the monochromator for collimation. Fluorescence-yield spectra at the Ni K-edge were collected using a 12-element energy-dispersive solid state Ge detector at 20-BM-B or a 100-pixel energy-dispersive monolithic Ge detector at 11-2. All data were calibrated using a Ni metal foil, with the first inflection point in the absorption edge set to 8333.0 eV. Measurements were made at room temperature with successive scans averaged to improve counting statistics. No systematic variations in spectra were observed with increasing X-ray exposure. Measurement of the background Ni speciation focused on the X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) region of the XAFS spectrum given the low solid-phase concentrations. Select samples containing added Ni also had data collected into the extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) region. Background subtraction, averaging, normalization, and linear combination fitting were done in the Athena interface to IFEFFIT. Structural analysis of EXAFS spectra was conducted in Sixpack using backscattering phase and amplitude functions generated in FEFF 7.02. The calculations used the crystal structures of mackinawite (FeS), with the central atom replaced by Ni, and nickel acetate tetrahydrate [Ni(CH3COO)2·4 H2O], with one Ni atom replaced by Fe, in both cases to provide compound-specific scattering functions for the relevant elements. S K-edge XAFS spectra were measured on SSRL beamline 4-3, which is equipped with a Si (111) double-crystal monochromator and a Si collimating mirror. Samples were cooled using a liquid He coldstream, with fluorescence data measured using a 7-element silicon drift detector. All data were calibrated to the first peak in sodium thiosulfate at 2472.02 eV.
X-ray Microfluorescence Imaging and Spectroscopy:
Thin sections of wetland soil from both field sites were prepared by first suspending soil material in Epo-Tek #301 epoxy in an anaerobic chamber. The Missouri soil was used as a coherent block, but the Florida soil lacked structural integrity and was added as small, homogenized fragments. The epoxy was added to each soil sample in a polyethylene beaker, which was then placed in a vacuum desiccator for 30 min to allow the epoxy to enter pore spaces. After solidification, the sample blocks were sent to Spectrum Petrographics (Vancouver, WA, USA) for preparation as 30 µm thin-sections mounted on quartz glass.
X-ray microfluorescence images were collected at SSRL beamline 2-3, which is configured with a Si (111) double crystal monochromoator and a pair of Kirkpatrick-Baez mirrors for focusing to a 5 µm spot. Images were collected using a 10.0 keV incident beam energy and a 4-element energy-dispersive silicon drift detector. The thin sections were also imaged at SSRL beamline 14-3 to explore the spatial distribution of sulfur species. This beamline uses similar optics at 2-3 with the sample maintained in a He-purged cell and the fluorescence signal is collected using a single-element silicon drift detector. Sulfur speciation maps were generated by collecting images of the same region of the thin section at multiple excitation energies near the sulfur K-edge: 2470.4, 2472.8, 2473.4, 2478.8, 2481.1, and 2500.0 eV for the Missouri soil and 2470.4, 2471.8, 2472.8, 2473.0, 2473.4, 2474.4, 2476.4, 2478.8, 2481.1, 2482.2, and 2500.0 eV for the Florida soil. In addition, S K-edge µ-XANES spectra were collected at select points of interest (POIs) to further explore the dominant sulfur species present and their spatial distributions. For all imaging experiments, full XRF spectra were recorded at each pixel and data were processed using the MicroAnalysis Toolkit package. Elemental correlations across full images were calculated for major elements, but similar analysis for trace metals is precluded by leakage of strong Fe fluorescence into the neighboring XRF region coupled to the low count rate in individual pixels for these elements. Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted on the multi-energy sulfur imaging data to explore the number of distinct species present. As for the bulk XAFS measurements, the µ-XANES spectra were processed and analyzed in the Athena interface to IFEFFIT.
